newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE-High hopes for Maori as NZ enters new era.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-High hopes for Maori as NZ enters new era.

text.p: New Zealand Maori, tired of losing out to whites in education, health and jobs, are striving for greater influence and a fairer deal as they prepare to vote in a general election next month.
Politicians are assiduously courting Maori, who make up 13 percent of the population, as the country goes to the polls on October 12 for its first election under proportional representation.

"The Maori vote now counts. They are a known block vote that is extremely loyal. Once the Maori vote is given to a party, it has a very long track record of being a very solid vote," said lawyer Donna Hall, a convenor of the pan-tribal Maori Congress.

Maori have five special seats reserved for them in an expanded parliament of at least 120 members, and they also occupy high-ranking places on the lists of all main parties. Analysts estimate a dozen or more could win seats.

"I think Maori have been cynical of the so-called democratic system for 100 years now, and so there was always a low Maori voter turnout," said Professor Ranginui Walker of Auckland University. "Now, suddenly, there's a renewed interest in the possibility that the democratic system really is going to be more democratic ... I've never seen such interest in an election from Maori as this one."

Optimism, however, is tempered by caution. Statistics paint a stark picture of the plight of Maori, a Polynesian people who reached New Zealand by canoe and settled here at least 1,000 years before Europeans arrived in the 18th century.
Maori unemployment is running at 14.4 percent -- down from nearly 20 percent two years ago but more than three times the rate among white New Zealanders, known as Pakeha.

Lower socio-economic status leads to poorer health. Maori are likelier to suffer cot death as babies, or catch meningitis or rheumatic fever as children. As adults, they are more at risk of heart disease, cancer and diabetes.
"At the end of the day, when Maori vote, they vote on employment, on health and on education matters," said Hall.
Less tangible to the average voter, but of key importance to Maori collectively, are the hundreds of claims outstanding for ancestral land that was seized by colonial settlers.

They resent as unfair and arbitrary a cap of NZ$1 billion (US$698,000) imposed by the current conservative government to settle all land claims under the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi, signed by their warrior ancestors with the British crown.

"That process is not about justice ... It's like throwing corn to a turkey. The turkey gobbles it up, and you shut the turkey up for a while," said Walker. "The government is seen to be doing something, so it wins brownie points with the dominant (white) side of the electorate, who wants these pesky Maori to disappear and these Treaty claims to come to an end."

Last year the government reached a major settlement with the North Island Tainui tribe, paying NZ$170 million and returning 15,790 hectares (39,000 hectares) of land. It has been pushing hard in recent weeks for a deal with a South Island tribe.
But the slow pace of progress and opposition to the $1 billion ceiling have fanned frustration among Maori radicals.
Protests last year, including the torching of an old school building and the 11-week occupation of a park in a North Island town, exposed tensions in New Zealand race relations.

"What we're on about is reaffirming our position as Maori in our own land and our own country. If that's radical, so be it," said Ken Mair of the small Mana Maori party, which advocates Maori "self-determination" as promised in the 1840 treaty.

Radicals such as Mair demand a separate Maori parliament, with powers to make laws for its own people. "It's not about turfing out the colonisers, it's about sitting down and working out the power relationships with each other," he said.

Other Maori politicians are more upbeat: they see improving race relations and a better chance than ever before for Maori MPs to work together as a caucus in the next parliament, cutting across traditional party rivalries.

"I do think the non-Maori community is far more ready than it ever was to settle those claims," said Donna Awatere Huata, a former radical who is standing as fourth-ranking candidate for the small free-market ACT party.
